clinicalPearls: One of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability, resulting from inadequate thyroid hormone at birth or in early infancy.
Most affected newborns appear normal at birth because of transplacental maternal thyroid hormone, so clinical detection is unreliable and newborn screening is essential.
The commonest cause worldwide is thyroid dysgenesis (aplasia, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland); dyshormonogenesis and, in some regions, iodine deficiency also contribute.
Later clinical features include prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, lethargy, constipation, a large fontanelle, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, and hoarse cry.
Screening measures TSH and/or T4 on a heel-prick sample; a raised TSH with low T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism.
Treatment is early thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine, and the key to normal neurodevelopment is starting therapy as early as possible.
Regular monitoring of growth, development, and thyroid function is needed to keep levels in the target range during infancy.
Delay in starting treatment is associated with irreversible loss of cognitive potential, making prompt recognition critical.
reference.pathophysiology: Thyroid hormone is essential for normal brain growth and myelination, particularly in the first years of life. In congenital hypothyroidism, deficient hormone production results from failure of thyroid gland development, an enzymatic defect in hormone synthesis (dyshormonogenesis), inadequate iodine substrate, or, less commonly, hypothalamic-pituitary (central) dysfunction. In primary disease, low circulating thyroid hormone removes negative feedback on the pituitary, raising TSH. Because maternal thyroid hormone crosses the placenta, the fetus is partly protected in utero, but after birth the untreated infant becomes progressively hypothyroid, and prolonged deficiency during the critical window of brain development produces permanent neurological injury.
additionalDifferentials: Transient neonatal hypothyroidism (e.g. maternal antithyroid drugs, iodine exposure, maternal antibodies)
Other causes of prolonged neonatal jaundice
Down syndrome and other conditions with hypotonia and feeding difficulty
Constitutional causes of poor feeding and lethargy
additionalInvestigations: Newborn screening TSH and/or T4 on heel-prick blood
Confirmatory serum free T4 and TSH
Thyroid imaging (ultrasound and/or radionuclide scan) to define aetiology
Maternal thyroid history and antibody status where relevant
Knee radiograph for bone age in some cases to assess in utero severity
redFlags: Positive newborn screen requiring urgent confirmation and treatment
Signs of significant hypothyroidism (marked lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia)
Delayed diagnosis beyond the early weeks of life, risking neurodevelopmental harm
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis through screening and prompt, adequately dosed replacement, neurodevelopmental outcome is typically normal; delayed or inadequate treatment risks permanent intellectual impairment.
pitfalls: Relying on clinical signs, which are usually absent or subtle in the newborn period
Delaying treatment while awaiting further tests once screening is clearly abnormal
Under- or over-treating due to infrequent monitoring during infancy
Missing central hypothyroidism when screening is TSH-based only
management: Start levothyroxine replacement as early as possible after a positive newborn screen to preserve neurodevelopment
Give crushed levothyroxine in a little water or breast milk, separated from soya feeds, iron and calcium that impair absorption
Monitor TSH and free thyroxine regularly and titrate the dose to growth and requirements
Developmental surveillance and hearing assessment to detect and address any deficits early
Thyroid ultrasound and radionuclide imaging to define aetiology and decide whether therapy is lifelong or can be trialled off later
Parental education on adherence and the harm of interrupted therapy
